chapter_theme: Under the heading அரசியல்பு, seventeen verses on the nature of kingship: punishing one's own and sparing no age, even justice to rich and poor, gentle taxation and the futility of favours paid for by extortion, the helplessness of subjects under an unjust king, the need for a measure of severity and a firm mind, keeping no rival power or equal close, not handing office to the unrestrained, forbearance as a ground of rule, and the gain of joining the great.

241.reading: The verse says that to think 'these are my own people' is a danger: even if they are one's own, a king who sees unfitting deeds must turn hard-eyed and punish, for a soft-eyed king who cannot punish will not rule.
241.nuance: தங்கண்ணர் puts kin and favourites inside the reach of punishment, and the proverb's மென்கண்ணன் turns the Kural's praised kindly eye (கண்ணோட்டம்) into a fault once it stops the rod.

pazhamozhi.literal: the soft-eyed man who cannot punish does not rule a kingdom

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who spares his own people

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king must punish wrong even in his own people

242.reading: The verse recalls that though the worthy hid and shielded the deed for long, even after the time had passed the father drove his chariot over the son who had driven over the calf of a milch cow, and proves by it that justice knows neither old nor young.
242.nuance: Lines 1-2 (கைகரப்ப, காலை கழிந்ததன் பின்றையும்) seem to say the elders concealed the son's deed and time went by, so the point is that neither concealment nor delay saved him; the exact sense of கைகரப்ப is not certain. The verse names neither the king nor the son.

pazhamozhi.literal: in justice there is no old age or youth

story.act: a father, the king, drove his chariot over his own son, who had run over a cow's calf, though the worthy had hidden the deed
story.tradition: identified by tradition as the Chola called Manu Needhi; the verse does not name him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king's justice does not spare the young, even his own son

243.reading: The verse says a king who knows justice must, without wavering, deal evenly with the rich and the poor, and that if he swerves and does not deal evenly it is like water flowing on one side and milk on the other.

pazhamozhi.literal: like water running on one side and milk running on the other

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who judges rich and poor unequally

pazhamozhi.applied_to: unequal justice gives the rich milk and the poor water from one source

244.reading: The verse says that for kings of unfading fitness and cool flower garlands, taking the wealth of those who live in the shade of their feet without hurting them, as if not taking at all, is the right taking, like the bee that eats the pollen and leaves.
244.nuance: The word division of the proverb (வண்டூதா துண்டு) is unsure; the image is in any case of the bee that feeds on a flower without harming it. அருத்தம் is the Sanskrit artha, wealth.

pazhamozhi.literal: as a bee eats from a flower and leaves it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's taking of his subjects' wealth

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king should take revenue so lightly that the subjects feel no loss

245.reading: The verse appears to say that even when the subjects live in prosperity, the king should not keep his levy over them excessively high, but take within the measure of his rule, since, as the proverb has it, milk does not keep welling beyond its measure.
245.nuance: Lines 3-4 are obscure: கோல்தலையே யாயினும் கொண்டீக may mean 'take and give, even at the sceptre's point' and பாலதலை is unclear, so both the instruction of line 3 and the proverb's image are my best guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: roughly, milk does not go on welling beyond (its) head; the image is unclear

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who presses levy on prosperous subjects

pazhamozhi.applied_to: prosperity does not license excess taxation

246.reading: The verse says that when a giving king harms those who came to him for refuge, turns crooked of sceptre, takes levy from his subjects beyond measure and then shows them favour, it is like cutting off a creature's crest and putting it in its own mouth.
246.nuance: The irony is in கொடைவேந்தன்: the king's generosity is paid for by the people he gives to, so his gift feeds them their own flesh. சூட்டு is most likely the cock's comb.

pazhamozhi.literal: cutting off the crest and putting it in the mouth

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king whose largesse comes from over-taxing his people

pazhamozhi.applied_to: favour funded by extortion only returns the subjects' own loss to them

247.reading: The verse asks, addressing the lord of the shore of swelling waves, what the subjects under the white umbrella can do if the king himself is not just, and answers that there is nothing: if the elephant itself takes the food and eats, there is no vessel that can cover it.
247.nuance: The white umbrella is the sign of protection, so the verse's point is that the protector turned taker leaves no higher recourse.

pazhamozhi.literal: if the elephant takes and eats, no vessel can cover the food

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to subjects under an unjust king

pazhamozhi.applied_to: against an unjust king the subjects have no protection

248.reading: The verse appears to say that for kings with rutting elephants, letting matters slip out of hand rather than keeping the upper hand over others is a danger, since even those who do penance rightly, like the bird that lives on raindrops, scorn the weak.
248.nuance: ஒளியாரை and கைகடத்தல் can be read more than one way (those who lack lustre or those who hide; to lose control or to overstep), so the counsel may be either 'keep the upper hand' or 'do not overstep except over the weak'. The rain-drinking bird is the cataka, an image of strict austerity.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who does not scorn the weak

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who lets his power slip

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king who appears weak will be scorned by all, even ascetics

249.reading: The verse says that if a king of great goodness, not divided in mind, acts with a firm mind, then what can hostile men do even if they gather an army with loud proclamations, for one stone is enough for a thousand crows.

pazhamozhi.literal: one stone for a thousand crows

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a resolute king facing a gathered enemy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a single resolute king scatters a numerous but weak enemy

250.reading: The verse tells a woman of bright bangles that even a king who bears the wheel of rule is scorned by his own allies if he is not just, and yet that kings need some harshness, however little, since even a cool stick, they say, makes the body rise.
250.nuance: The verse holds two things together: injustice earns contempt, and a measure of வெங்கோன்மை is still needed. The proverb's sense (that a light rod still raises welts, or still makes one stand up) is not certain. ஆழியான may be the wheel-bearing emperor or Vishnu.

pazhamozhi.literal: even a cool stick, it is said, raises the body

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the measure of severity a king must keep

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king needs a little severity even within just rule

251.reading: The verse asks the lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea, where the water leaps over the punnai, how others could gain the upper word under a king's command, since a tree does not grow under a tree.

pazhamozhi.literal: a tree does not grow under a tree

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to rivals for power under a king

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no second authority can rise under a king's rule

252.reading: The verse appears to say, to a woman of bamboo shoulders, that those who made strong the men who served them can destroy or raise them as they will, like water held in the cheek, which one may slowly swallow or spit out.
252.nuance: The proverb is only கவுட்கொண்ட நீர், and பாத்தறிவென் மெல்ல is unclear; my reading takes the water in the mouth as wholly at the holder's disposal.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to followers a ruler has raised

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those a ruler has raised remain his to make or unmake

253.reading: The verse tells a woman of soft shoulders that for a king to keep men who aspire to leadership on an equal footing with himself is like living with a snake in one room.
253.nuance: நிலைமையால் நேர்செய்து may mean raising them to equal rank or keeping them level with one another; either way the danger is ambitious men kept close and strong.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of living with a snake in a single room

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king who raises would-be leaders to his own level

pazhamozhi.applied_to: rivals given equal standing are a constant danger at close quarters

254.reading: The verse appears to say, to a woman whose smile is like jasmine, that as Death when it takes a life does not stop to examine those who have pleas, so there is nothing one can do when the king suddenly seizes one.
254.nuance: It is unclear whether the verse warns the subject that royal power is as deaf as Death or reproaches a king who seizes without inquiry; வல்லை (quickly) and அரசாட் கொளின் allow both.

pazhamozhi.literal: what can one do if the king swiftly seizes (one)

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a man caught by royal power

pazhamozhi.applied_to: against the king's sudden seizure there is no plea, as against Death

255.reading: The verse says that to place the high dignity of great wealth on a man of unrestrained mind who is not upright in conduct is to put a firebrand in a monkey's hand.
255.nuance: ஒளளியன் is probably a slip for ஒள்ளியன், so 'not upright (or not wise) in conduct'. The proverb's monkey will not keep the fire still, so the damage spreads beyond the man himself.

pazhamozhi.literal: giving a firebrand into a monkey's hand

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to giving high office to the unrestrained

pazhamozhi.applied_to: power given to the unrestrained spreads ruin

256.reading: The verse says that those who do not quickly grow angry even at those who did them boundless harm are the ones said to rule the world, and people, drawn in by their words, take shelter at their feet like a food-bearing tree in a field.
256.nuance: ஒல்லை வெகுளார் is 'not angry quickly', not 'never angry'; the forbearance is of speed. The shelter image, கூழ்மரம், is my reading of a tree whose yield feeds those near it.
256.domain_note: the forbearing as those who rule the world

pazhamozhi.literal: like a food-bearing tree in a field

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the forbearing ruler around whom people gather

pazhamozhi.applied_to: slowness to anger draws people to a ruler's shelter

257.reading: The verse recalls that the younger brother of Lanka's lord came over himself as ally to Rama of the garland and gained even the kingship of Lanka, and proves by it that none who joined the great and held close to them failed.
257.nuance: The epic case cuts against kin loyalty: the reward comes from leaving his brother for the great one, and the verse passes no judgment on that.

pazhamozhi.literal: there are none who joined the great and held close to them who did not thrive

story.act: the younger brother of Lanka's lord went over to Rama as his ally and was made king of Lanka
story.tradition: the younger brother is Vibhishana in the Ramayana tradition; the verse names only Rama

pazhamozhi.applied_to: joining and keeping close to the great brings gain, even a kingdom

links.note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting without favour to anyone; Pazhamozhi 241 names the hardest case of that 'anyone', one's own people.
links.teaches: The couplet's யார்மாட்டும் is abstract; the pairing shows where impartiality is actually tested, at the king's own kin, and names the failure there as softness of eye.
links.list_adds: its proverb turns கண்ணோடாது into a portrait of the king who fails it, the soft-eyed man who cannot punish, so the rule gains a named vice the couplet does not give.

links.note: 241 demands that the king turn hard-eyed and punish; 256 praises rulers who are not quickly angered even by great harm.
links.teaches: Together the two separate severity from haste: the king must punish wrong without favour, but the rulers people shelter under are those slow to anger at harm done to them.

links.note: Kannaki cites the Chola who crushed his own son under the chariot for a cow's grief; Pazhamozhi 242 tells the same episode and adds that the worthy had hidden the deed.
links.teaches: Kannaki uses the episode to shame a king who killed without inquiry; Pazhamozhi makes it a rule about age, so one exemplum serves both as indictment and as maxim.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 6 has a young Chola who judges well despite his youth; 242 has a son not spared despite his youth.
links.teaches: Read together the two Chola stories make youth irrelevant from both sides of the court: it neither disqualifies the judge nor excuses the accused.

links.note: Kural 118 praises leaning to no side like a level balance; Pazhamozhi 243 applies that to the king's dealing with rich and poor and pictures the lean as milk and water.
links.teaches: The couplet's balance shows only that something tilts; the pairing names who gains and loses, the rich getting milk and the poor water from one royal source.
links.list_adds: it moves the worthy man's balance into the king's court and names the two parties, rich and poor, that the couplet leaves unnamed.

links.note: Pisirandhaiyar tells the Pandya to take his due like an elephant fed paddy in balls, not one loosed in the field; Pazhamozhi 244 gives the same rule of revenue through the bee that takes and leaves.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem warns one king of the ruin a greedy collection brings on him and his land; the ethics verse lifts the warning into a general rule of royal taking that should leave no mark at all.

links.note: 245 says even prosperous subjects should not bear excess levy; 246 says a king's favours funded by excess levy are like feeding a creature its own crest.
links.teaches: The two close both escapes for over-taxing: the subjects' prosperity does not justify it, and the king's later generosity does not redeem it.

links.note: Kural 552 likens a sceptred king's demand to a robber's 'hand it over'; Pazhamozhi 246 follows the extorted wealth into the king's gifts.
links.teaches: The couplet stops at the taking; the pairing shows the robbery disguised as largesse, so a king can be both robber and giver at once.
links.list_adds: it sets refuge-seekers harmed, crooked rule, excess levy and later favour in one sequence, so the extortion of 552 is followed to its use.

links.note: Muthumozhikkanchi 26 says those under an unjust king do not openly censure him; Pazhamozhi 247 says they have no recourse at all.
links.teaches: The pair gives the reason for the silence: the people do not speak against the unjust king because, with the protector himself the taker, there is no one higher to cover them.

links.note: 248 says a king who lets things slip is scorned, since all scorn the weak; 250 says an unjust king is scorned by his own allies and yet needs some severity.
links.teaches: Together they place the king between two contempts, for weakness and for injustice, and make a small severity within just rule the way between them.

links.note: Kural 763 says a host of rats roaring like the sea perish at the cobra's breath; Pazhamozhi 249 says a gathered enemy army is nothing to a firm-minded king, one stone for a thousand crows.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the strength in the cobra alone; the pairing traces it to the king's undivided mind, so numbers fail against resolve, not only against force.
links.list_adds: its condition, a king not divided in mind, gives the source of the one's power over the many that the couplet's image takes for granted.

links.note: Kural 562 tells the king to raise the rod sharply and bring it down lightly; Pazhamozhi 250 says kings need a little harshness, since even a cool stick raises the body.
links.teaches: Both refuse a choice between mildness and terror, and the pairing shows two ways to split it: the couplet splits the act into threat and blow, the quatrain sets a small severity inside just rule.
links.list_adds: it adds the cost of failing at the other end, that even allies scorn a king who is not just, so severity is fenced by contempt on both sides.

links.note: 251 says no rival word can rise under a king's command, as no tree grows under a tree; 253 says keeping would-be leaders on equal footing is living with a snake.
links.teaches: 251 states the fact of single authority and 253 the danger of breaking it, so together they explain why a king keeps the ambitious beneath him.

links.note: 252, on a doubtful reading, says a ruler can unmake the men he raised; 253 warns that men raised to equal standing are a snake in the room.
links.teaches: Read together, 253 limits the confidence of 252: the raised follower stays in the ruler's hand only while he is not raised to the ruler's level.

links.note: Kural 890 says living with those not in accord is like dwelling with a snake in a hut; Pazhamozhi 253 uses the same image for a king who keeps aspirants to leadership on his own level.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves open who the discordant companions are; the pairing names them in a court, ambitious men the king himself has raised, so the snake is one he brought in.
links.list_adds: it carries the household image into the king's domain and makes the king's own act of raising men the cause of the danger.

links.note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Pazhamozhi 255 says giving high dignity to the unrestrained is putting a firebrand in a monkey's hand.
links.teaches: The couplet counts the folly as the king's; the proverb shows it burning outward, since the monkey with fire harms everything near it, not only the one who handed it over.
links.list_adds: it moves the fault from ignorance to want of restraint and adds wealth to the trust given, so the harm is power and means in an unruly hand.

links.note: Kural 155 says the world keeps the forbearing like wrapped gold; Pazhamozhi 256 says the slow to anger rule the world and people shelter under them like a food tree.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the forbearing esteem; the pairing turns esteem into rule, so forbearance is shown as a ground of authority and not only of reputation.
links.list_adds: its image reverses the couplet's direction: the forbearing are not kept by others like gold but keep others under their shade.

links.note: Kural 443 says making the great one's own is the rarest of things; Pazhamozhi 257 shows Lanka's younger prince joining Rama and gaining Lanka.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks the act as rare; the pairing gives its reward in one epic case, and shows the bond with the great outweighing even the bond with a brother.
links.list_adds: it proves the couplet's claim by a story, and the story's cost, leaving a brother, is something the couplet's general claim does not face.

source_issues: 243: the comparison site lacks this verse (show flag site_diff).
245 line 4: பாலதலை is obscure, and line 3 கோல்தலையே யாயினும் கொண்டீக is unclear.
247 lines 3-4: the quotation opens inside மற்றில்லையே (மற் 'றில்லையே), splitting a word; the proverb's own words are probably யானை தொடுவுண்ணின் மூடுங் கலம் with இல்லை.
252 lines 3-4: the quotation opens after மெல்ல at கவுட்கொண்ட நீர், and பாத்தறிவென் is obscure; the bounds of the proverb are doubtful.
255 line 3: ஒளளியன் is probably a typing slip for ஒள்ளியன்.
